results.title: Should systematic reviews and meta-analyses include data from preprints? - PMC
results.content: # Should systematic reviews and meta-analyses include data from preprints? As attentive observers of the rapidly developing literature on the effect of the Covid-19 pandemic in mental health, we have been witnessing an interesting conundrum: should systematic reviews and meta-analyses include data from preprints in their results? They found that, on average, the quality of reporting is slightly better for peer-reviewed journal articles compared to preprint articles. Compared to peer-reviewed articles, preprint articles were less likely to report conflicts of interest, funding sources, and unit-level (most commonly individual people) data. These data are not in accordance with other studies which did not find significant differences between the two versions.5-7 Conflicts of interest are a very relevant variable which is commonly used in sensitivity analyses in meta-analyses of interventional studies.8 It should be noted that preprint repositories have recently changed their policy for reporting conflicts of interest, with medRxiv requiring disclosure of conflicts of interest, while bioRxiv was not requiring it at the time the study by Carneiro et al. performed a methodological research study of systematic reviews and meta-analyses in medicine.10 Their aim was to investigate if including unpublished data would have an impact on results. 3. Possibility of conflicting information between the preprints and the final form of the published article (e.g. authorship, additional analysis, discussion of the results). Future approaches to this topic could include the obligation to disclose conflicts of interests, funding, and unit-level data in preprints, a better description of the search strategy in the preprint datasets, improvement of the advanced search tools for the preprint datasets, standardized analysis of the quality of the gray literature and preprints, inclusion of additional exploratory analysis of peer-reviewed and not peer-reviewed material, and, finally, a balanced discussion of the impact of inclusion of these two types of literature on future systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Comparing quality of reporting between preprints and peer-reviewed articles in the biomedical literature. Systematic review finds that study data not published in full text articles have unclear impact on meta-analyses results in medical research.

results.content: They aim to measure study quality and use these scores in meta-analysis. Understanding **quality scoring** helps researchers improve the validity and reliability of their findings. * Weighted **quality scoring** systems aim to quantify the methodological rigor of individual studies and incorporate these scores into the meta-analysis, preserving the core purpose of meta-analysis while accounting for variations in research quality. * Understanding the nuances of quality scoring is crucial for researchers to make informed decisions and enhance the validity and reliability of their meta-analytic findings. Quality scoring in research is key to checking if study results are real and reliable2. In meta-analysis research, weighted quality scoring is a detailed way to look at different studies4. Researchers use different tools to check the quality of studies in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Checking the quality of research studies is key in meta-analysis. > “Subjectivity in quality scoring can lead to inconsistent evaluations across different reviewers, while variability in quality assessment tools poses challenges in comparing results across meta-analyses.”. By tackling these challenges, we can make quality scoring in meta-analysis more reliable. *The weighted scoring model is a powerful tool that can greatly improve the quality and reliability of meta-analysis research. **Quality scoring methods** have made health research more reliable. It’s key to check how well quality scoring methods work in different fields for meta-analyses17. Weighted quality scoring is crucial in meta-analysis. As we wrap up our look at quality scoring in meta-analysis, it’s clear that making these systems better is key. Tailoring these methods to fit each research field can make them more useful and improve meta-analysis quality22. As meta-analysis grows, so does the need for better quality scoring methods22. These advancements are key for improving *quality scoring improvement*, *meta-analysis best practices*, and *research methodology advancements*22. Researchers looking into quality scoring, meta-analysis, and research methods will find lots of useful information. results.title: Grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions - PubMed
results.content:
Title: Grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions - PubMed
# Grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions. # Grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions. The inclusion of grey literature (i.e. literature that has not been formally published) in systematic reviews may help to overcome some of the problems of publication bias, which can arise due to the selective availability of data. To review systematically research studies, which have investigated the impact of grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions. A study was considered eligible for this review if it compared the effect of the inclusion and exclusion of grey literature on the results of a cohort of meta-analyses of randomized trials. Information was also collected on the area of health care, the number of meta-analyses, the number of trials, the number of trial participants, the year of publication of the trials, the language and country of publication of the trials, the number and type of grey and published literature, and methodological quality. All five studies showed that published trials showed an overall greater treatment effect than grey trials. This showed that, on average, published trials showed a 9% greater treatment effect than grey trials (ratio of odds ratios for grey versus published trials 1.09; 95% CI 1.03-1.16). Overall there were more published trials included in the meta-analyses than grey trials (median 224 (IQR 108-365) versus 45(IQR 40-102)). The most common types of grey literature were abstracts (55%) and unpublished data (30%). There is limited evidence to show whether grey trials are of poorer methodological quality than published trials. This review shows that published trials tend to be larger and show an overall greater treatment effect than grey trials. Sally Hopewell is the author of one of the studies included in this review and Matthias Egger is author of another of the included studies, which was published as a NHS Health Technology Assessment review. Comparison 1 Grey versus published trials, Outcome 1 Estimates of treatment effect. ##### Burdett 2003 {published and unpublished data}. ##### Egger 2003 {published and unpublished data}. ##### Fergusson 2000 {published and unpublished data}. ##### Bhandari 2000 {published data only}. ##### Horn 2000 {published data only}.

results.title: Diagnostic Performance of Diffusion-Weighted Imaging for Colorectal Cancer Detection: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - PMC
results.content: # Diagnostic Performance of Diffusion-Weighted Imaging for Colorectal Cancer Detection: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. ### Aim. To investigate the diagnostic value of DWI-MRI quantitative analysis in colorectal cancer detection. Studies published in English that used DWI-MRI for diagnosing colorectal cancer were included. The performance of DWI-MRI for diagnosing colorectal cancer was accurate, with pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio, and negative likelihood ratio of 0.88 (95% CI = 0.85–0.91), 0.92 (95% CI = 0.91–0.94), 30.36 (95% CI = 11.05–83.43), and 0.44 (95% CI = 0.30–0.64), respectively. **Keywords:** colorectal cancer, diagnostic performance, DWI, MRI, sensitivity, meta-analysis. Several recent studies (7–10) have demonstrated that DWI provides high-contrast resolution morphological imaging, thereby significantly improving the diagnostic accuracy of colorectal cancer by MRI. Therefore, we conducted this meta-analysis to investigate the diagnostic performance of DWI-MRI for colorectal cancer detection. Studies were eligible for inclusion in this meta-analysis if they fulfilled the following criteria: 1) cases with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of colorectal cancer; 2) colorectal cancer detection or staging by DWI-MRI; 3) studies providing sufficient raw data to construct a 2 × 2 contingency table to perform MRI sequences; 4) studies published in English; and 5) for studies conducted using the same study participants, the most recent publication or the one with more detailed information was included. The current study systemically explored the diagnostic accuracy of DWI in detecting colorectal cancer. Another meta-analysis (11) investigated DWI for colorectal cancer detection and showed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.95 (95% CI = 0.90–0.97) and 0.93 (95% CI = 0.85–0.97), respectively. Moreover, the small sample sizes also limited further subgroup analyses or sensitivity analyses, e.g., only a few studies on colon cancer were available, and MRI with DWI was reported to have a better performance in detecting more colonic cancers than CT (36).
